claims.text: Sub-solvus aging will induce a uniform dispersion of coherent nanoscale precipitates in a BCC refractory high-entropy alloy matrix.
The precipitate dispersion will enhance high-temperature strength and creep resistance.
The aging treatment will preserve the alloy's low density.
The aging treatment will preserve room-temperature ductility.
Refractory high-entropy alloys commonly have a BCC matrix.
The proposed starting alloy has acceptable room-temperature mechanical properties but insufficient high-temperature performance.
Adding heavy refractory elements can impose a density penalty.
The aging temperature should be slightly below the precipitate solvus and the hold time should be optimized.
The treatment will produce coherent nanoscale precipitates such as an L1_2 or similar phase within the BCC matrix.
Coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion during high-temperature loading.
Impeded dislocation motion will improve strength retention and creep resistance.
Because aging does not alter the nominal composition, it should cause no appreciable density increase.
The nanoscale and coherent character of the precipitates will keep room-temperature ductility largely unaffected.
Relative to an as-cast or solutionized baseline, the aged alloy will have significantly higher yield strength and lower creep rate at 1000–1200 °C.
Relative to the baseline, the aged alloy will maintain similar room-temperature tensile strength and ductility.
Aging too far outside the optimized sub-solvus range can cause insufficient precipitation or precipitate coarsening and compromise the benefit.
Optimal aging temperature and duration may vary with alloy composition and processing history.
The hypothesis is falsified if aging yields no statistically significant improvement in high-temperature strength and creep resistance, or measurably degrades room-temperature strength or ductility.
